# Social posts — week of 2026-06-15 (next-few-days batch)

Working draft. **Rewrite the posts marked `REWRITE`** (the blog + 2 course posts) in your own voice; leave the `READY` ones or tweak as you like. When you're done, tell me and I'll convert this into the 3-platform batch JSON at `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/next-few-days.json`, condensing each post to LinkedIn / Mastodon (<=500) / Bluesky (<=290).

Conventions when I build the JSON: the URL goes in the `url` field (no UTM, no inline links; the pipeline adds per-platform UTM), and `image` stays `""` (the pipeline scrapes og:image).

**Posting order:** the pipeline schedules in array order, 3 posts/weekday at 10:00, 13:30, 15:30 ET. The order below interleaves AI and Scrum so no day is all one theme. Reorder by moving blocks.

---

## 1. Blog — false consensus — REWRITE
**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/

You hand the team a clean list of GenAI-generated user stories.

They read them. They nod. They say "yes, I understand."

And every person is picturing something different.

That's the trap with using GenAI to write your user stories, epics, or acceptance criteria. These artifacts were never the point. They exist to help people to reach a shared understanding through conversation. When the story arrives looking finished, the conversation never happens, and you get false agreement that falls apart as soon as the work starts.

This predates GenAI. Product Owners could always bash out a polished product backlog item and mistake nodding for understanding. GenAI just manufactures that false consensus faster.

Where can GenAI help in Refinement: ask it to pressure-test a story. Does it meet INVEST? Is the "why" clear? Where's the ambiguity? Stuck splitting something big? Have it suggest splits. Most of them will be wrong, but it can be a good spark. Let it question your prioritization.

The difference: those uses spark the conversation. Generating the stories replaces it.

I use these tools daily. Knowing where they erode shared understanding is how you use them well.

How GenAI fits across all five Scrum events and activities:

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

---

## 2. Evergreen — Daily Scrum — READY
**URL:** /blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/

The Daily Scrum isn't a status meeting, and the moment it becomes one, it dies.

Three people reciting yesterday-today-blockers at a ScrumMaster is reporting, not planning. The point is the team re-planning the day together toward the Sprint Goal: what we learned, what changed, where we help each other.

If yours feels like a chore, the format is the problem, not the people.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

---

## 3. Quiz — confidence trap — READY
**URL:** /quiz/ai-failure-modes/

Microsoft researchers (2025) found something uncomfortable: the more confident an LLM sounds, the less critical thinking people apply to what it says.

Confidence is the trap, and it's only one of the failure modes quietly shaping how teams build software right now.

How well do you know the AI Failure Modes hitting Development Teams? Test yourself. Twelve questions, three minutes.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Course — glass 1/3 full — REWRITE
**URL:** /surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/

Most of the AI conversation hands you two options.

The glass is overflowing: AI replaces your engineers next year, so go as fast as you can. Or the glass is empty: it's all hype and harm, avoid it.

If neither fits what you're seeing, you're not alone. I'd put the glass at about a third full. GenAI is genuinely useful. Every day I use Claude Code to make drudge work get done with less effort.
It's also far more complicated than the marketing claims, happy to turn a 15-minute task into a 3-hour rabbit hole. Both are true.

You're a ScrumMaster, Product Owner, or team member being asked to make this work, without a reliable way to tell the real third from the noise. That's the gap Surviving the AI Tsunami is built to close.

Six weeks, evidence-based, working real problems from your own team. You'll leave able to put GenAI where it earns its place and leave it out where it doesn't.

Beta cohort starts June 29. Have a look:

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Evergreen — Sprint Goals — READY
**URL:** /blog/sprint-goals-provide-purpose/

"Finish these seven stories" is not a Sprint Goal. It's a to-do list with a deadline.

A real Sprint Goal names the outcome you're after, so when reality shifts mid-Sprint the team knows what to flex and what to protect. Without one, every surprise becomes an argument about scope instead of a decision about value.

Purpose first, backlog second.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 6. Evergreen — code, not so fast (glass 1/3 full) — READY
**URL:** /blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/

"It feels faster" is not the same as "it is faster."

In one study, seasoned devs using GenAI on familiar code came out 19% slower than without it, while certain they were speeding up. Self-reported productivity and measured throughput barely correlate.

I'd put GenAI coding tools at about a third full: real value, well short of the hype. Worth using, not worth trusting on feel. Measure the real thing, Cycle Time and Throughput, before you believe the speed.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 7. Quiz — don't decide on vibes — READY
**URL:** /quiz/ai-failure-modes/

Mandates are landing on desks. Productivity claims are getting louder. Almost no one is bringing the actual research to the conversation.

Three minutes from now you could be the rare person in your org who knows how GenAI actually fails, instead of deciding on vibes.

Test your knowledge of AI Failure Modes in Development Teams. Twelve questions, real citations.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 8. Evergreen — Story Mapping — READY
**URL:** /blog/drowning-in-oversized-product-backlog-story-mapping-is-your-life-raft/

A 150-item backlog isn't a plan. It's where good ideas go to be forgotten.

Story Mapping pulls it back into something human: the user's journey across the top, the slices of value underneath. Suddenly you can see what's essential, what's a first release, and what can quietly wait.

If your backlog has become an archive nobody trusts, map it.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 9. Evergreen — human cost (glass 1/3 full) — READY
**URL:** /blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/

A research finding that's easy to miss: GenAI can make people more productive and less motivated at the same time.

More output, less ownership of it. For a Scrum team, motivation and shared understanding aren't nice-to-haves, they're the engine. Trade them for raw speed and it's a poor deal.

I read GenAI here as about a third full: genuinely useful for the dull work, oversold on the rest. Use it there, and protect the conversations that keep people invested.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

---

## 10. Course — the mistake — REWRITE
**URL:** /surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/

I shipped a side project with every receipt image left publicly exposed. I teach this for a living, I was being careful, and I still missed it.

I mention it because the people being pushed to ship faster with GenAI right now aren't careless. They're careful people working under pressure, with tools that make mistakes easy to create and hard to spot.

If that's you, the goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well: knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell the difference.

That's what we work on in Surviving the AI Tsunami. I'm not there as a guru with the answers. I'm the guide who has made the mistakes and can help you skip a few. You bring real problems from your team, we work them together over six weeks.

# Reclaimed post drafts (from Drafts inbox, 2026-07-11)

Three older post drafts pulled out of the Drafts backlog during the weekly review. Evergreen-eligible; rewrite in your voice before scheduling. Two reference already-published blog posts (likely promo), one is an engagement poll.

---

## 1. AI-label poll (engagement) — captured 2026-02-24

I'm not an AI Techno-optimist. I'm not a pessimist either. I use these tools every day. I see real value and the harm in them. I see the hype >> reality.

What I want to be is the person you trust to share both sides, the good and the bad. Someone mapping the territory as it actually is, not as vendors promise it will be.

I've been searching for a label that captures that middle ground. Three candidates:

- AI Cartographer - mapping the terrain, cliffs and all
- AI Sherpa - trusted guide through difficult, uncertain territory
- AI Surveyor - measuring what is really on the ground

Which one resonates? Tell me why you voted, or suggest something better.

(I'm not abandoning Agility. Being Agile is necessary for surviving this mess.)

---

## 2. Feature Factory + a superpower (promo) — captured 2026-02-23
**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/

Imagine giving a Feature Factory a superpower. Not the power to understand customers better. Not the power to measure outcomes. The power to ship features faster.

That's what GenAI does for teams already stuck in the output trap.

The original Feature Factory symptoms (rigid roadmaps, no discovery, velocity obsession, ignored tech debt) were never caused by building too slowly. They were caused by not stopping to think. AI doesn't fix that. It removes the last natural speed bump that might have forced a conversation about value.

When code was expensive to write, teams at least had to prioritize. When AI makes it cheap, everything gets built. The backlog becomes a conveyor belt.

The antidote is the same as it always was, focus on outcomes, but now AI can actually help:

- ScrumMasters: push for experiment-driven Sprints. Instead of "build feature X," frame the Sprint Goal as "learn whether X solves problem Y." Use AI to stand up a quick prototype or Fake Door MVP.
- Product Owners: use the speed AI gives you to validate faster, not ship faster. Run three small experiments in the time it used to take to build one feature.

AI is a superpower. The question is whether you use it to produce more, or to learn faster.

---

## 3. Product Owners: ease of use > shiny AI features — captured 2026-02-18

GenAI is making it easier and easier to migrate providers for various tools. I'm getting increasingly frustrated with our current email marketing platform. I'm trying to use APIs more, and I've learned most of the product's features are only accessible via the GUI.

I've already written code to extract our entire newsletter archive + stats. When the time comes, I'll export the remaining content without much manual labour.

When I did the first survey, I found Canadian and EU providers (data sovereignty) are much cheaper and provide full API access.

The irony: the provider in question has been adding AI features I don't need, rather than making it easier for me to use their product in the first place.

Product Owners, we don't need more shiny AI features. Ease of use is more important.

# Weekly Review

Step back, look at the week, and plan the next one.

## When to Use

Run this once a week — Sunday evening, Monday morning, or whenever works for your rhythm.

## Instructions

### Step 1 - Gather
1. Check this week's calendar events (if calendar MCP is connected).
2. Review completed tasks or projects from the week.
3. Scan any notes, journal entries, or captured items from the past seven days.
4. **Email digest via the Gmail MCP** (see `Skills/gmail-triage.md` for conventions). Report counts per category - don't list individual emails unless Mark asks. Use `search_threads`:
   - Important unread (7d): `is:unread is:important in:inbox newer_than:7d`
   - Primary/people unread (7d): `is:unread in:inbox category:primary newer_than:7d`
   - Notifications unread (7d): `is:unread in:inbox category:updates newer_than:7d`
   - Newsletters (7d): `in:inbox category:promotions newer_than:7d`

   (Meeting-transcript listing retired with Spark; there is no Gmail equivalent.)
5. **APR analytics check.** Ask Mark if he wants to run `apr-weekly-analytics` as part of the review. If yes, invoke it and fold the findings into Step 2. If skipped, note when analytics were last refreshed (look at the modified date on `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`).
6. **Writing Kanban review.** Open the APR Kanban view mentally - ask Mark which items he wants to commit to this week. Convert commitments into OmniFocus tasks via `omnifocus-capture`. The Kanban stays as idea pool + writing-capture; the weekly picks go to OmniFocus.
7. **Marketing Experiments check.** Skim `APR/Analytics/Experiments/_Experiments Index.md` for active experiments. Flag any whose monitoring dates have arrived.
8. **Repo work recap (what shipped).** Read-only git history across Mark's APR repos to summarize the week's shipped work. Repos:
   - APR astro (website): `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro` (usually the bulk of the work; descriptive commit messages)
   - social-media-posting: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/social-media-posting` (evergreen/batch posting tooling; low volume)

   **Excluded - LifeHQ-Mark** (`/Users/marklevison/Documents/Obsidian/LifeHQ-Mark`): a global deny rule blocks Read/Edit/Write on it (set in `~/.claude/settings.json`), and it is all "Autocommit" vault backups anyway. Do not try to read it. If Mark asks why it is missing, point at the deny rule.

   For each repo, run (use `git -C <path>`, not `cd` - `cd` resets the shell cwd and can trip a permission prompt):
   ```bash
   # Commit list with messages
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --date=short --pretty=format:"%ad | %s"
   # Per-commit scope, for sizing the work
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --pretty=format:"%h %s" --shortstat
   # Area churn (which folders moved the most)
   git -C <repo> log --since="<start> 00:00" --pretty=format: --name-only \
     | grep -v '^$' | sed 's:/[^/]*$::' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30
   ```
   Default window is the last 7 days (today minus 7); honor an explicit range if Mark gives one. Then:
   - Group commits into 2-5 themes per repo (e.g. email/CRM, funnel/quiz, sales pages, analytics refresh, course logistics). Lead with outcomes, not commit subjects.
   - Flag big diffs that are data churn (analytics dumps, generated PDFs, dependency removals) so they do not read as feature work - e.g. a "delete Drip" commit removing ~15,800 lines is cleanup, not net-new build.
   - Do not dump raw commits unless Mark asks; fold the recap into the "Shipped This Week" output section.
9. **OmniFocus inbox sweep.** Run `omnifocus-inbox-triage` to clear the OmniFocus inbox — walk each item, propose a project (plus tags/due/flag as needed), and apply approved edits as a batch. See `Skills/omnifocus-inbox-triage.md`. Skip if the inbox is empty; note the count either way.
10. **Drafts review and cleanup.** Run `drafts-inbox` to process the Drafts inbox — read each captured item, take the action, and archive when done. See `Skills/drafts-inbox.md`. Skip if the inbox is empty; note the count either way.
11. **Content Ideas resurfacing.** Read `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` and surface 2-3 hooks for Mark to consider promoting into Writing Tasks (`APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/`) or this week's plan. Rotate which ones you highlight so the whole list stays in view over time. Skip if the note is empty or missing.

### Step 2 — Review
1. Summarize what happened this week: key events, completed work, progress made.
2. Identify what's still open: tasks that didn't get finished, items that slipped.
3. Flag anything overdue or time-sensitive.

### Step 3 — Output
Produce a formatted weekly summary **in chat only**. This is an in-the-moment review — do not save it to a file, and do not ask reflective questions.

**Weekly Review — [Date Range]**

**What Happened**
[Key events, accomplishments, completed work.]

**Shipped This Week (Repos)**
[Per-repo themed bullets from the git recap, busiest repo first. One net line per repo (files, insertions, deletions) where it helps. Skip a repo with no commits in the window but say so in one line. LifeHQ-Mark excluded.]

**Email**
[Unread counts by category for the week. Skip if the Gmail MCP isn't connected.]

**Inboxes Processed**
[One line each for the OmniFocus inbox sweep and the Drafts inbox review: how many items were processed (or "empty"). Note any that need a follow-up decision.]

**Content Ideas to Consider**
[2-3 hooks pulled from `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md`, rotated week to week. Skip if the note is empty.]

**Still Open**
[Unfinished items, slipped tasks, things that need attention.]

**Next Week**
[Upcoming calendar events, deadlines, priorities.]

## Customization Ideas

This is a starter weekly review. As you use it, consider adding:
- Role-based review (how did each area of your life/work get attention?)
- Goal tracking (progress toward monthly or quarterly goals)
- Automated data gathering from connected tools

The assembler in Video 7 will help you customize this to your actual workflow and connected tools.

## Rules

- This is an in-the-moment review for Mark's use during the session. Deliver it in chat only — do not save it to a file or create a notes folder for it.
- Don't ask reflective questions ("how did the week go," "what to adjust"). Just present the gathered review.
- Keep the output scannable. Short lines, clear sections.
- If data sources aren't connected, work with what's available. A review based on the user's verbal summary is still valuable.
- The repo recap is read-only: only `git log` / `git diff` reads. Never commit, edit repo files, or `git add`.
- Never read or write LifeHQ-Mark. It is blocked by a global deny rule; do not work around it.
- For the repo recap, group commits into themes rather than dumping the commit list, and label large data-churn diffs so they do not read as feature work.

---

*Started with the Robot Assistant Field Guide Starter Kit. Customized in Video 7 via the assembler.*

   - Notifications unread (7d): `is:unread in:inbox category:updates newer_than:7d`
   - Newsletters (7d): `in:inbox category:promotions newer_than:7d`
